docs.title: When should I follow this course?
docs.text:
When you need to create a plot and accept to use ggplot2 to do so.

Especially at the start of any new programming language, having help is very useful: some error messages seem like complex, yet have simple solutions. A teacher helps you get past those first errors.

docs.title: When should I consider to not follow this course?
docs.text: These are the reasons to consider to not follow this course:

docs.title: Reason 1: you want to learn advanced things
docs.text:
When you have written your first scripts in R and expect to learn new and more advanced things.

In this case, the course will go too slow for you.

However, you will probably be put to work by the teachers to help out other learners. If you like to test your own knowledge by teaching others, you will likely thrive in the course.

docs.title: Reason 2: you have social anxiety
docs.text:
When you have social anxiety.

In this case, the course will be too social for you.

However, in this course, it is perfectly OK to give a wrong answer or to say 'I do not know'. This is what a former learner had to say on this:

You are welcome to try and leave anytime you want. The course material is made for self-study too, with videos for all exercises. Do fill in the evaluation when you leave early :-)

docs.title: Why is the course learner-centered?
docs.text:
Because that is good teaching.

This course defines good teaching as 'evidence-based methods to let learners acquire new skills and the monitoring of this acquisition'. This means that it should be observed that learners need more/less to time to practice and following the schedule based on that. Learner-centered teaching has an effect size from 0.36 [Hattie ranking] or 0.64/0.70 [Cornelius-White, 2007][Hattie, 2012].

Or: it is useless to go faster than the learners can follow. Lecturing is known to negatively affect learning [Hattie, 2023].

The teaching methods of this course follow the evidence-based teaching cycle by [Bell, 2020a], which allows learner-centered teaching.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• ggplot2 uses a grammar of graphics for plotting

  • ggplot2 expects tidy data

  • Using ggplot2:

ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point()
  • Saving a ggplot, directly after plotting:
ggsave("my_filename.png")
  • R uses the arrow operator for assignment
my_variable <- 3.14
  • swirl can be used as a tool to learn R
library(swirl)
swirl()
  • Use readr to load data from a file
library(tidyverse)
read_csv("my_data.csv")

docs.title: A typical project visualization
docs.text:
You want to visualize past and predicted population size by country, using the data from the Wikipedia article 'World population'

These are the steps:

  • 1. Preparing the data
  • 2. Reading the data
  • 3. Tidying the data
  • 4. Cleaning the data
  • 5. Saving the plot
  • 6. Refine

docs.title: 1. Preparing the data
docs.text:
You (wisely) decide to start with only a subset of the data from the Wikipedia article 'World population':

Country 2000 2015 2030 China 1270 1376 1416 India 1053 1311 1528

From the context, you understand that:

  • the columns with numbers (e.g. 2000) is the years
  • the values in the cells are the estimated population size, in millions

This data is best saved as a comma-separated (.csv) file.

In RStudio, create a new text file: click on 'File | New File | Text File'.

Where do I need to click?

Click on 'File | New File | Text File':

You now have created an empty text file called Untitled1.

What does that look like?

Your screen looks similar to this:

China,1270,1376,1416
India,1053,1311,1528
What does that look like?

Your screen looks similar to this:

Save this file by clicking 'File | Save'.

Where do I need to click?

Click on 'File | Save':

When asked for a name, type population_sizes.csv and click 'Save'.

docs.title: 3. Tidying the data
docs.text:
The data must be transformed to be tidy, which holds these features:

  • Each variable is a column; each column is a variable.
  • Each observation is a row; each row is an observation.
  • Each value is a cell; each cell is a single value.

Our data is not tidy yet:

Country 2000 2015 2030 China 1270 1376 1416 India 1053 1311 1528

Our data is not tidy yet, as we have three observations per row:

  • The population in each in the year 2000
  • The population in each in the year 2015
  • The population in each in the year 2039

In R, we can make this tidy in many ways, for example:

library(tidyr)
t <- t |> pivot_longer(
  cols = c("2000", "2015", "2030")
)

Add this code at the end of the create_plot.R script and run it.

You can now observe that t is tidy like this:

Country name value China 2000 1270 China 2015 1376 China 2030 1416 India 2000 1053 India 2015 1311 India 2030 1528 Where do I need to click to see t again?

Double-click on t here:

Transforming the data is described in:

  • Chapter 3: Data Transformation
  • Chapter 5: Data Tidying

docs.title: 4. Cleaning the data
docs.text:
Now we need to do some data transformations:

names(t) <- c("country", "t", "n")
t$country <- as.factor(t$country)
t$t <- as.numeric(t$t)

Add this code at the end of the create_plot.R script and run it.

What does that look like?

This looks similar to this:

What we have just done:

  • We set the column names of t to country and t and n
  • We set the country column to be categorical: countries are categorical, in this case, either India or China. The technical term is that a country is a factor. Using factors is described in Chapter 16: Factors
  • We set the t column to be numeric, as years are numbers

Now the data looks like:

country t n China 2000 1270 China 2015 1376 China 2030 1416 India 2000 1053 India 2015 1311 India 2030 1528

Plotting this now works:

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(t, aes(x = t, y = n, color = country)) + geom_line()

Add this code at the end of the create_plot.R script and run it.

What does that look like?

This looks similar to this:

docs.title: 5. Saving the plot
docs.text:
After having plotted the plot, it can be saved as such:

ggsave("my_plot.svg")
ggsave("my_plot.png")

Add this code at the end of the create_plot.R script and run it.

docs.title: 6. Refine
docs.text:
The plot looks like this now:

You can refine it in many ways:

  • Refine the SVG in another tool
  • Refine the generation of the plot

For example, in R:

ggplot(t, aes(x = t, y = n, color = country)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous("Time (year)") +
  scale_y_continuous("Population size (million)", limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(title = "Population size in time", color = "Country")

Add this code at the end of the create_plot.R script and run it.

Now the plot has proper labels:

Refining the looks of your plot is described in:

  • Chapter 11: Communication

docs.title: This course setup
docs.text:
• This workshop is aimed at learners from any initial skill level.
  • We use R: this seems to be most common in this course
  • We use R's ggplot2 library: this is the most used plotting library in R and it is very tunable
  • We use a free book, so that you can learn R and ggplot2
  • We use breakout rooms, so we can talk in small groups
  • You can work alone or in a group of two/three
  • Breaks are sacred, the schedule is not Advanced learners will likely finish earlier. Beginner learners will get the extra time and help they need.
  • You are encouraged to leave when you are done and having filled in the course evaluation. Do say bye: it is the human thing to do
  • You can always leave feedback anonymously that will be published: this helps improve the course

Sometimes I will ask for a 'Yes' or 'No' reaction. Here is where you can find these in Zoom:

docs.title: Why use R?
docs.text:
• R is a Turning-complete programming language
  • R is widely used: it is among the top 10 most used programming languages and probably among the top 2 of programming languages used in academia
  • R is a free and open-source language
  • R works on all major operating systems
  • R has many packages: a package is a body of code written by others that you can use easily. Currently, there are around 25,000 general packages and around 2,000 packages specialized for the life sciences. Whatever you are looking for, R probably has a package for just that!

docs.title: Why use ggplot2?
docs.text:
• ggplot2 is an R package for plotting
  • ggplot2 is widely used: it is among the top 100 most downloaded R packages
  • ggplot2 has the most commonly used plots available, e.g. those showcased in this gallery
  • ggplot2 has many extensions to plot even more, e.g. those showcased in this gallery
  • ggplot2 uses a grammar of graphics, which allows you to express your plotting needs in code
  • ggplot2 can create publication-ready plots: you will start recognizing them :-)

docs.title: Why use the book 'R for Data Scientists'?
docs.text:
• The book 'R for Data Scientists' is about using R and ggplot2 to visualize data
  • The book is free and open access
  • The book is both digital and in paper
  • The book follows best practices, e.g. the Tidyverse approach

docs.title: Before teaching
docs.text:
While preparing, I already concluded to call this a workshop.

  • [ ] Call this a workshop

Besides that, one weakness I will discover later, is that originally I started with the book, then moved to the general workflow overview. I reversed that. This had two negative consequences:

  • The learners were more ill-prepared to do the exercises: they had not created an R script yet, etc
  • That session was not updated to reflect the (lower) starting point

docs.title: During teaching
docs.text:
During teaching I spoke to the course coordinator. She stated that the purpose of this workshop is not only to create a plot, but also to discover the possibilities of R and ggplot2. At that time, I said we'll talk about it later.

At 9:10 I found out that all learners had already installed RStudio and the tidyverse packages. I decided to skip that section and I am happy with that decision.

docs.title: After teaching
docs.text:
I have mixed feelings about how the teaching went.

What I liked is how most learners started exploring and working as intended. Some were done early and finished early: that is great, so that I can give more time to the beginners.

Also, I have spoken to all learners and helped them at each level. Some learners already have the higher-level questions, such as how to clearly communicate a message using a plot.

I was unhappy with the session to create a data file: this had too little detail for beginners. I should show how to do this in RStudio. Because of the lack of guidance, people used Excel, which gave new problems: in Swedish Excel, exporting to a CSV results in values separated by a semicolon (i.e. not a comma)! This needlessly slowed around 4 learners down.

  • [x] Describe in more detail how to create a data file
  • [x] Describe in more detail how to create an R script

Also, to most learners it was unclear what the goal was of this session.

  • [x] Describe in more detail the goal of this session
  • [ ] Consider to demo this section

docs.title: Before teaching
docs.text: After teaching on the first day, I reflected. Today, due to that, I added the 'Why is R important?' and 'Why is ggplot2 important?', as well as a demo to the schedule. It felt like fixing my own teaching. I think it is interesting that have missed this important part of a lesson. That I missed this is easy to explain: my private life feels rushed and too-little-time too.

docs.title: During teaching
docs.text:
I did the two better-late-than-never sections at the start, then I let the people that want to work in their breakout rooms, while others would see the demo. The majority stayed. Then I did the demo. This went smoothly, except for copy-pasting into the Zoom chat: it sometimes took ten seconds to load. I used the Slack as a backup for pasting quickly.

I asked some learners if the demo was useful and if I should do that demo on day 1. One stated that the demo was useful, but day 1 would be too early. Another stated that the demo was useful and that it should have been on day 1.

  • [x] do the demo on day 1

I think I should do the demo on day 1, so I added this to the schedule to remind me.

Such opposite opinions reflect the diversity of the group well: it had everything from complete beginners to not-really-needing-to-be-there experts.

After the demo, I went through all the rooms. I noticed I had created too few rooms, so some learners cramped together in a room first, and later moved to fill up a vacant room.

At around 10:30 around three fourth of the learners were already asking questions about how to communicate clearly with a plot. At around 11:30, I understood from the last learner that he/she had a plot, so my mission has been successful.

docs.title: After teaching
docs.text:
I never felt connected to my teaching these two days, in the way that I usually do. Sleep will fix this.

It was an interesting experience, with a mix of

  • A diverse group
  • Problems due to a mismatch between the bigger and my course
  • An unexpected second learning outcome
  • all (?) learners achieving the goal

I will evaluate in a bit more detail with the course coordinator on Friday.

docs.title: Evaluation results
docs.text:
A lot of ""I am cool and enthusiastic and flexible and do what you want"" show and a little too little orientation over the course contents / the plan / the to dos -> I found the freedom not engaging but confusing. Please record lectures in the future for 2x option (even though I do understand that the way it is structured now, it does not really make sense to record it, because there is no content to record, but then the label ""lecture"" in the schedule is maybe not the best description of what it is)"

I agree that there is a lot of freedom. I think what would help improve this is to first offer a structure in general, then offer flexibility in breakout rooms for those that need it, like I do in all (?) other courses I teach. I love the quote 'I found the freedom not engaging but confusing' and I will use it as a reminder to myself.

I also agree that the start was not done well and I have already improved that.

I agree that 'lecture' would be a misnomer. Taking a look at the schedule, there is no mention of the word 'lecture'. Maybe this learner would also agree with me that 'course' is a misnomer and that it should be called a 'workshop' instead. Aha, now I get it: my workshop is put in the bigger course's schedule as a lecture!

  • [ ] Ask the course coordinator to refer to my sessions as a workshop

It was a good repetition of R theoretical part, I could work on my own pace. Help was available if needed.

Great!

I had no previous experience in using R and I feel that in just two morning i managed to learn the very basics with plotting a graph. I feel that there should have been at least a small lecture where the teacher was going throught the very basics (how your data should look like on excel, or how to save your R script for example). I found these two hours fun and this increased my interest in learning how to use R better

I agree with this learner and I think he/she missed the lecture on day 2 (that should have been given on day 1), where I did most of these suggestions. I enjoy the tip about reading Excel: I've seen more people using it. As this is a very diverse group of people, it would help those that need it.

  • [ ] Add how to read Excel data

I think It would be good at the beginning of the course to make a more clear distinction between the experience people have with Rstudio, to make it less frustrating for the people who have not tried it before and also make better groupings ind the zoom-rooms. This would make it easier for people to get what they need out of the course and also have better discussions with people on the sample level - to generalte ideas for how to display data.

I agree that it should have been more clear that the course provides for learners of all levels. I have already updated this in the course material, but maybe I should make this even more explicit, for example, by grouping people on experience level.

  • [ ] Consider grouping on experience level.

I have created some kind of plot, but I had to figure most of it out on my own, with the help of AI... It had been very helpful for a beginner like me to have the introduction to R Monday morning (not Tuesday). It had saved me some anxiety at least.

I am happy we agree that I should have done that presentation on day 1. It would indeed make life less stressful.

Richel is a friendly teacher to interact with, which makes the learning much more fun and easy!

Great to hear.

docs.title: 6. Verbatim Student Submissions
docs.text:
There are some responses that are quite negative against me. I am fine with that: I am happy that the learners speak their thoughts. Within the course, the R sessions is a bit of an outlier: (1) it is a minor part of the course (2) the main audience (i.e. people that are attracted to do graphical visualisations) may not be attracted to programming, (3) the learners are expected to work (unlike the other minor parts in the course, where they are only expected to listen). Due to this, me and the course leader expect most negative feedback to go to this part of the course.

  • Not really, keep it as it is. This was the first KI course I recommend to other PhD students.
  • I think it would be great if during week to the students were devided into groups of who have experience with Rstudio and who do not have.

Great idea! Me and the course leader already agreed to do so too :-)

  • Because as somebody with experience I used a lot of time on helping with the basics and I think that because I was not prepared for this I did not know how to do it properly - to lessen the students in my groups frustation of learning a completly new program. So I could have used my time better by talking and developing ideas for my data visulization if I had been in a group where people have experience and the one i 'helped' could have learned it better if they had gotten a structred teaching on Rstudio.

I wish I understood better what happened here. I never ask my learners to take over teaching. I do ask them to help each other. I do see (and saw here too) that some learners start teaching. And I feel this is a good thing: the learners have some freedom on how to engage with each other and I should be generous on how they should do so. However, what happened here is not what I wanted; that a learner started taking over teaching. I do usually spot this, when I can navigate the breakout rooms more often. I predict I will be able to circle around more often if I do day 1 properly.

What I do know, is that the plan to differentiate between learners has already been accepted. I hope that that will resolve this issue.

  • The R session was very confusing and disorienting. Working with a book does not need to happen in breakout rooms. Very irritating teaching style in terms of the way we were spoken to, in my opinion.

These are different ideas. I think working with a book should happen in breakout rooms. My teaching style is annoying for passive learners and I will accept any criticism from that.

I do agree that I could have done a better job and have already decided to do so before these evaluation results came in. I hope that that will fix this.

  • I personally find that the homework needs more than the planned time, especially to get use to a new software. It could have been a bit more credit hours.
  • Richel Bilderbeek was not the perfect teacher for a total beginner in R! I would have wanted some introduction and some tips and tricks how to at least get started. (He did not teach med R, AI did.)

I agree I am not the perfect teacher, as there is no such thing as a perfect teacher. I am happy to read I have been successful in creating a learning environment where he/she used AI to learn: this is -no pun intended- perfect: we have some initial evidence that AI tutors seem to be more effective at teaching than humans [Kestin et al., 2025]! I think that there should have been a demo on the first day and this has already been updated in the course schedule.

  • The description could be a little bit more clear. I misinterpreted it somewhat. Quite overwhelming for someone who has never worked with vector programs or R before.
  • It might be better to have the possibility to have education IRL during the practical sessions. Difficult to get help online.
  • They should allow the use of elements from Biolender
  • The DataVis practice on the Wednesday of the 2nd week felt very repetitive, especially the group parts in breakout rooms, after we had talked a lot about data visualisation. Maybe it should be earlier in the course. I also didn't find the lectures on Thursday very useful, there wasn't much tangible information in there, more like 'hey be aware those things exist and look into them'.
  • I also would suggest making people plot the same data for the 2 data visualisations, it makes it more interesting to compare how to communicate in scientific publications and to a general audience.
  • Even though graphical design skill were not required, it would be good to mention it in the syllabus. It was a bit stressful in the beginning.
  • Maybe the R software part could be a bit more redesigned / flexible to include multiple softwares for those who are not using R frequently.

Yes, we will divide the beginners into groups.

  • Would be nice to add a section on which graphs / visuals can work better to convey the message and impacts for different types of data.
